title: From woman we are born
hook: Guru Nanak asks why she should be called lesser, from whom kings are born (Asa di Var, ang 473)
tomorrow: Ask about the light, not the caste

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kirtan Sohila's first hymn. Your line was the date is written. Did you make the call you'd been putting off? Today, a short verse with a very sharp question in it. Day two hundred forty-seven.

Picture the Punjab five hundred years ago. In many homes, and in many religious customs of the time, a woman who had just given birth was treated as unclean for days. Some said women couldn't reach the highest spiritual goals at all. It was simply how things were said. Then a traveling teacher with a musician at his side sings a verse that asks one question, so plainly that it's hard to argue with. It's in the Asa di Var, the morning ballad, and today we hear it: from woman we are born.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO.` → `WOMEN CALLED UNCLEAN, LESSER.` → `ONE PLAIN QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The Asa di Var is a long hymn sung in many gurdwaras in the early morning. On Ang 473 comes a salok by Guru Nanak. It begins with a drumbeat of one word, bhand, woman. In paraphrase: from woman we are born; in woman we are conceived; to woman we are engaged and married. Woman is our friend; through woman the family goes on. When one woman dies, a man seeks another; through woman come our bonds with the world. And then the question, in the original: so kio mandaa aakheeai jit jameh raajaan. Why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? The salok goes on: from woman, woman is born; without woman there is no one at all. Only the One, the True Lord, Nanak says, is beyond woman. Notice where this sits. The verses just before it are about the idea of ritual impurity, sutak, the belief that birth made a house unclean. Guru Nanak answers that impurity lives in greed, lies and gossip, not in a newborn or a mother. So this isn't a greeting-card compliment. It's an argument, set right in the middle of a debate about who is clean. Sikh practice built on it. The Gurus taught that women and men sit together in the sangat, eat together in the langar, and may read from the Guru Granth Sahib and lead prayers. Many Sikhs will tell you, honestly, that life hasn't always matched the verse. But the verse is there, sung every morning, still asking.
screen: `ASA DI VAR — THE MORNING BALLAD.` · `BHAND: BORN, MARRIED, BONDED.` · `WHY CALL HER LESSER?` · `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT WHO IS CLEAN.` · then, large: `WHY CALL HER LESSER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a woman in your life: a mother, a grandmother, a sister, a friend, a teacher, a colleague. Picture her face. Think of one thing she carried that nobody thanked her for. Hold that for a moment. Then decide one small way to honor her today: a message, a thank-you, credit given out loud. Rest with the breath, and keep her in mind. The bell holds the time.
From woman we are born. Guru Nanak's salok in the Asa di Var: everyone comes through woman, so why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?
screen: `FROM WOMAN WE ARE BORN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: why call her lesser. Today, honor one woman in your life, out loud, for something she's never been thanked for. Day two hundred forty-seven.

fork.setup: people around Guru Nanak say a house is made unclean by a birth. what does the Asa di Var answer?
options: that they're right, and women should keep apart.
that impurity lives in greed, lies and gossip, and asks why she should be called lesser, from whom kings are born.
fork.reveal: Guru Nanak moves impurity from the body to behavior, then asks: so kio mandaa aakheeai jit jameh raajaan.

original.note: Gurmukhi: bhand, an old Punjabi word for woman; the salok repeats it like a drumbeat.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about mothers.
what it means: a sharp question: everyone is born through woman, so why call her lesser?
what a scholar hears: a salok of Mahala 1 in the Asa di Var (Ang 473), following saloks on sutak, ritual impurity; bhand is an old word for woman used here with deliberate repetition.
